Twisted-pair copper is cheap and common in LANs but suffers interference and is limited to about 100 metres per run. Bandwidth is the capacity of a channel; bit rate is the number of bits actually sent each second. Transfer time equals the number of bits divided by the bit rate.

Serial transmission sends bits one after another along a single channel and works reliably over long distances. Parallel sends several bits at once but suffers skew and crosstalk, so it is used only over short distances.

Simplex sends in one direction, half-duplex in both directions but not at once, and full-duplex in both directions simultaneously. Synchronous transmission uses a shared clock and sends continuous blocks; asynchronous transmission frames each character with start and stop bits.

A cyclic redundancy check divides the data by a fixed polynomial and checks the remainder, detecting burst errors reliably. Automatic repeat request corrects errors by retransmission: the receiver sends acknowledgements, and the sender resends any block that is negatively acknowledged or whose acknowledgement does not arrive in time.

Bandwidth?
The capacity of a communication channel (range of frequencies), which determines the maximum rate at which data can be transmitted.
Bit rate?
The number of bits transmitted per second over a communication channel.
Full-duplex?
A transmission mode in which data can travel in both directions at the same time.
Asynchronous transmission?
Transmission without a shared clock, where each character is framed by start and stop bits.
Parity bit?
An extra bit added to a group of bits so that the total number of 1s is even (even parity) or odd (odd parity), used to detect errors.
Cyclic redundancy check (CRC)?
An error-detection method in which a remainder calculated by dividing the data by an agreed polynomial is sent and checked by the receiver.
